title: An argument from natural reason: what preservation needs, first production needs still more
source_text: VIII. Illis vero Scripturae sacrae testimoniis addunt etiam argumentum a ratione naturali petitum, sic enim ratiocinantur. Nullae substantiae creatae in rerum natura permanere possunt, nisi Deus illas immediate influxu suo conservet; multo magis ergo simili influxu egent substantiarum motus & actiones: quomodo enim verum esse posset accidentia minus a Deo pendere ad sui conservationem quam ipsas substantias? Cum vero id quod ad conservationem rei est necessarium, majori cum ratione necessarium sit ad primam ejusdem rei productionem, inde consequens est ut nihil omnino a causis secundis valeat produci, nisi simul actualis immediatusque influxus causae primae interveniat.
pass_a_gloss: But to those testimonies of sacred Scripture they add also an argument sought from natural reason, for thus they reason. No created substances can remain in the nature of things, unless God preserve them immediately by his influence; much more therefore do the motions and actions of substances need a like influence: for how could it be true that accidents depend less on God for their preservation than substances themselves? But since that which is necessary to the preservation of a thing, is with greater reason necessary to the first production of the same thing, it is consequent thence that nothing at all can be produced by second causes, unless at the same time an actual and immediate influence of the first cause intervene.
pass_b_english: To these scriptural testimonies they add an argument from natural reason, which runs as follows. No created substance can continue to exist unless God keeps it in being by his immediate influence. Much more, then, do the motions and actions of substances need such influence, for how could accidents depend less on God for their preservation than substances do?

Moreover, whatever a thing needs in order to be kept in being, it needs all the more in order to be produced in the first place. It follows that secondary causes can produce nothing whatever unless an actual and immediate influence of the first cause is present at the same time.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.
